title: The Spirit given in different measure
source_text: Καὶ τί με δεῖ ἐπὶ πλεῖον ἀντιπαρατιθέναι τῇ λέξει Κέλσου. ὡς πολλῷ πρότερον τούτων παρ᾿ ἡμῖν λελεγμένων, ὅτε καὶ ἐκ τῶν εἰρημένων σαφές ἐστι τὸ βούλημα ἡμῶν; ἐν τούτοις δὲ καὶ οἱονεὶ τίθησιν, εἰπὼν πνεῦμα θεῖον κατιὸν ἐκ θεοῦ προαγγέλλειν τὰ θεῖα, τοῦτ᾿ ἂν εἴη τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ταῦτα κηρύττον. οὗ δὴ πλησθέντες ἄνδρες παλαιοὶ πολλὰ κἀγαθὰ ἤγγειλαν. οὐκ εἶδε δὲ διαφορὰν τῶν παρ᾿ ἡμῖν ἠκριβωμένων. τοῖς λέγουσιν ὅτι καὶ „τὸ ἄφθαρτόν σου πνεῦμά ἐστιν ἐν πᾶσι. διὸ τοὺς παραπίπτοντας κατ᾿ ὀλίγον“ ἐλέγχει ὁ θεὸς, φάσκουσι δὲ ἄλλα καὶ τὸ „λάβετε πνεῦμα ἅγιον“ τὴν ποσότητα τοῦ διδομένου ἑτέραν ἐμφαίνειν παρὰ τὴν δηλουμένην ἐκ τοῦ „βαπτισθήσεσθε ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ οὐ μετὰ πολλὰς ταύτας ἡμέρας.“ ἔργον δέ ἐστι ταῦτ᾿ ἐπιμελῶς νοήσαντα ἰδεῖν διαφορὰν τῶν ἐκ διαλειμμάτων πλειόνων χωρησάντων τὴν τῆς ἀληθείας κατάληψιν (καὶ) βραχεῖαν ἐπίνοιαν θεοῦ καὶ τῶν ἐπὶ πλεῖον θεοφορηθέντων καὶ ἀεὶ μετὰ θεοῦ ἑστηκότων καὶ διὰ παντὸς ὑπὸ θείου πνεύματος ἀγομένων· ὅπερ εἰ ἦν ἐξετασθὲν καὶ νενοημένον Κέλσῳ, οὐκ (ἂν) ἀμαθίαν ἡμῖν ἐνεκάλει οὐδὲ προσέταττε μὴ λέγειν τυφλώττειν τοὺς ἐν ὑλικαῖς τέχναις ἀνθρώπων, ταῖς κατὰ τὰ ἀγάλματα, οἰομένους ἐνδείκνυσθαι τὴν εὐσέβειαν. οὐδεὶς γὰρ βλέπων τῆς ψυχῆς ὀφθαλμοῖς ἄλλῳ τρόπῳ σέβει τὸ θεῖον παρὰ τὸν ὑποδεικνύντα ἐνορᾶν ἀεὶ τῷ τοῦ παντὸς δημιουργῷ καὶ πᾶσαν εὐχὴν ἀναφέρειν ἐκείνῳ καὶ πάντα πράττειν ὡς ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖς θεοῦ, ἐπὶ θεατοῦ, ἐνορῶντος ἡμῶν καὶ τοῖς λογισμοῖς. εὐχόμεθα οὖν ἡμεῖς καὶ βλέπειν καὶ ὁδηγοὶ εἶναι τυφλῶν, ἕως προσελθόντες τῷ λόγῳ τοῦ θεοῦ ἀπολάβωσι τὰς ὑπὸ τῆς ἀγνοίας τυφλωθείσας ὄψεις τῆς ψυχῆς αὐτῶν. ἐὰν δὲ καὶ ποιῶμεν ἄξια τοῦ εἰπόντος τοῖς μαθηταῖς· „ὑμεῖς ἐστε τὸ φῶς τοῦ κόσμου“ καὶ τοῦ διδάξαντος λόγου ὅτι „τὸ φῶς ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ φαίνει,“ ἐσόμεθα καὶ „φῶς“ τῶν ἐν σκότει καὶ παιδεύσομεν τοὺς ἄφρονας καὶ διδάξομεν τοὺς νηπίους.
pass_a_gloss: And why must I (δεῖ) further set against (ἀντιπαρατίθημι) the passage (λέξις) of Celsus, as these things having been said among us much earlier (πρότερον), when also from what has been said our intention (βούλημα) is clear (σαφής)? In these (words) he also as it were posits (οἱονεὶ τίθησιν), saying [that if] a divine spirit (πνεῦμα θεῖον) descending (κάτειμι) from God foretells (προαγγέλλω) divine things, this would be the spirit proclaiming (κηρύττω) these things, filled (πίμπλημι) with which ancient men announced (ἀγγέλλω) many good things. But he did not see the difference (διαφορά) of the things worked out precisely (ἀκριβόω, perf. pass.) among us by those saying that also 'your incorruptible (ἄφθαρτος) spirit is in all; therefore those falling aside (παραπίπτω) little by little (κατ᾿ ὀλίγον)' God convicts (ἐλέγχω), and asserting (φάσκω) among other things that 'receive holy spirit' shows (ἐμφαίνω) the quantity (ποσότης) of what is given (δίδωμι) as different from that shown by 'you will be baptized (βαπτίζω) in holy spirit not after many these days'. It is a task (ἔργον) having understood (νοέω) these carefully (ἐπιμελῶς) to see the difference of those who from rather many intervals (διάλειμμα) received (χωρέω) the apprehension (κατάληψις) of the truth and a brief (βραχύς) notion (ἐπίνοια) of God, and of those more fully god-borne (θεοφορέω) and always standing (ἵστημι, perf.) with God and continually (διὰ παντός) led (ἄγω) by divine spirit; which, if it had been examined (ἐξετάζω) and understood by Celsus, he would not charge (ἐγκαλέω) us with ignorance (ἀμαθία), nor order (προστάσσω) not to say that those are blind (τυφλώττω) who in material (ὑλικός) crafts (τέχνη) of men, those concerning statues (ἄγαλμα), think to display (ἐνδείκνυμι) piety (εὐσέβεια). For no one seeing with the eyes of the soul reveres (σέβω) the divine (τὸ θεῖον) in another manner than the one showing (ὑποδείκνυμι) [how] always to look upon (ἐνοράω) the craftsman (δημιουργός) of the all and to bring up (ἀναφέρω) every prayer (εὐχή) to him and to do all as in the eyes of God, before a spectator (θεατής) looking into even our reasonings (λογισμοί). We pray (εὔχομαι) then both to see and to be guides (ὁδηγός) of blind, until, having approached (προσέρχομαι) the word (λόγος) of God, they receive back (ἀπολαμβάνω) the sights (ὄψις) of their soul blinded (τυφλόω) by ignorance (ἄγνοια). And if we also do things worthy (ἄξιος) of the one who said to the disciples 'you are the light of the world' and of the word (λόγος) having taught (διδάσκω) that 'the light shines (φαίνω) in the darkness (σκοτία)', we shall also be 'light' of those in darkness (σκότος) and shall train (παιδεύω) the senseless (ἄφρων) and teach the infants (νήπιος).
pass_b_english: And why should I go on setting parallels against Celsus’s text, since these things were said among us long before, and our meaning is already plain from what has been said? In these words he also, as it were, grants that if a divine spirit coming down from God foretells divine things, “this would be the spirit that proclaims these teachings, filled with which men of old announced many good things.” But he did not see the distinction carefully drawn among us by those who say that “your incorruptible Spirit is in all things; therefore” God corrects “little by little those who go astray” (Wisdom of Solomon 12:1–2), and who also say, among other things, that “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22) shows a different measure of what is given from the one shown by “You will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now” (Acts 1:5).

It takes real effort, once these things have been carefully understood, to see the difference between those who, at long intervals, received a grasp of the truth and a brief notion of God, and those who were more fully inspired by God, who always stood with God, and who were at all times led by the divine Spirit. Had Celsus examined and understood this, he would not have charged us with “ignorance”, nor would he have told us not to call blind those who think they show their piety in the material crafts of men, the crafts that make statues. For no one who sees with the eyes of the soul worships the Divine in any other way than the way that shows us how always to keep our eyes on the Maker of the universe, to offer every prayer to him, and to do everything as in the sight of God, as before a spectator who sees even into our thoughts.

We, then, pray both to see and to be guides of the blind (Romans 2:19), until they come to the Word of God and recover the eyes of their soul, which ignorance has blinded. And if we also act worthily of him who said to the disciples, “You are the light of the world” (Matthew 5:14), and of the word that taught that “the light shines in the darkness” (John 1:5), we shall also be “a light” to those in darkness (Romans 2:19), and we shall train the foolish and teach the immature (Romans 2:20).

choices.choice: Celsus’s sentence is given in full at 7.45 (καὶ πνεῦμα εἴ τι οἴεσθε κατιὸν ἐκ θεοῦ προαγγέλλειν τὰ θεῖα...); the staged text here lacks εἴ τι οἴεσθε and Origen introduces it with οἱονεὶ τίθησιν (‘lays down as it were’), so it is rendered as a conditional supposition, with Celsus’s main clause in quotation marks. ‘These teachings’ (ταῦτα) are the Platonic doctrines Celsus has just quoted. The sentence οὐκ εἶδε δὲ διαφορὰν τῶν παρ᾿ ἡμῖν ἠκριβωμένων τοῖς λέγουσιν is read as one clause (dative of agent with the perfect passive), against the staged full stop after ἠκριβωμένων. Wisdom 12:1–2 is quoted with the verb ἐλέγχεις turned into the third person (ἐλέγχει ὁ θεός). (καί) before βραχεῖαν and (ἂν) before ἀμαθίαν are editorial supplements, accepted. ‘Ignorance’ and ‘not to call blind’ answer Celsus at 7.45 (τὴν ἑαυτῶν ἀμαθίαν ἐγκαλύπτετε καὶ μὴ λέγετε τυφλώττειν τοὺς βλέποντας); Origen applies the phrase to image-worshippers, so only ‘ignorance’ is set in quotation marks. τοῦ διδάξαντος λόγου is taken as ‘the word (of Scripture) that taught’, lowercase; it could also mean the divine Word, John’s speaker. Romans 2:19–20 (ὁδηγὸν εἶναι τυφλῶν, φῶς τῶν ἐν σκότει, παιδευτὴν ἀφρόνων, διδάσκαλον νηπίων) is said ironically by Paul of the boastful Jew; Origen takes the phrases over as a Christian task. Review: ἀντιπαρατιθέναι with no object rendered ‘setting parallels against’ (Origen has been setting Scripture beside Plato’s words quoted by Celsus); οἱονεὶ τίθησιν rendered ‘as it were, grants’. In Wisdom 12:2 ἐλέγχει stands outside the quotation, so ‘God corrects’ is set outside the marks; ἐλέγχω there means ‘correct, reprove’, not ‘convict’. νηπίους rendered ‘the immature’ (Romans 2:20 ‘teacher of the immature’).
first clause: 'set anything more against ... to show' changed to 'setting parallels against ..., since' (ὡς + genitive absolute is causal, not purpose)
οἱονεὶ τίθησιν: 'lays down, as a kind of supposition' -> 'as it were, grants'
Wisdom 12:2: ἐλέγχει 'convicts' -> 'corrects'; quotation marks now match the Greek (verb outside); παραπίπτοντας 'fall away' -> 'go astray'
ἔργον ... νοήσαντα ἰδεῖν: participle now prior ('once these things have been carefully understood')
